title: Conjecture 21
context_text: Let $P=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d : A\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b}\}$ be a polytope given by $A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times d}$ and $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{Q}^m$. A circuit of $P$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{g}$ such that $A_I\mathbf{g}=0$ for some $(d-1)\times d$ submatrix $A_I$ of $A$ of rank $d-1$ (all edge directions are circuits; for polygons, i.e. $d=2$, circuits are exactly the edge directions). A circuit move from $\mathbf{x}\in P$ goes to $\mathbf{x}+\alpha\mathbf{g}$ for a circuit $\mathbf{g}$ with $\alpha>0$ maximal such that the point stays in $P$, and a circuit walk of length $k$ is a sequence of $k$ circuit moves. The problem Circuit Distance takes as input such a polytope, two vertices $\mathbf{s}$ and $\mathbf{t}$ of $P$ and an integer $k\ge0$, and asks whether there is a circuit walk from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ of length at most $k$. Circuit walks underlie circuit augmentation schemes for linear programming, which generalize the simplex method. The authors prove that the monotone variant (walks that strictly improve a linear objective $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{x}$ at each step and end at a $\mathbf{c}$-maximal vertex) is NP-hard already for polygons, and even NP-hard to approximate within $m^{1-\varepsilon}$; they remark that their techniques seem likely to extend to the non-monotone setting, but this requires some technical innovation. This is discrete geometry / optimization rather than graph theory.
notes: Polygons are 2-dimensional polytopes; in this case circuit directions coincide with edge directions (as noted in Observation 9 of the paper).
paper_title: Short circuit walks in fixed dimension
